summary: The note describes how cats, known in ancient Egypt as "Mau", were regarded as sacred in Egyptian society. It summarizes genetic evidence that cats were first domesticated from the Middle Eastern wildcat subspecies about 10,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent. It also notes that later Egyptian peoples practiced a religion centered on animal worship, including cats.
one_line: Overview of how cats, called Mau, were sacred in ancient Egypt, with their domestication origins in the Fertile Crescent.
key_facts: Cats (Felis silvestris catus) were known in ancient Egypt as "Mau".
Cats were considered sacred in ancient Egyptian society.
Based on recent DNA comparisons of living species, cats were estimated to have been first domesticated from the Middle Eastern subspecies of the wildcat.
Cats were estimated to have been first domesticated about 10,000 years ago.
Cats were first domesticated in the Fertile Crescent.
Thousands of years after domestication, the peoples in what would later be Upper and Lower Egypt had a religion centering on the worship of animals.
The animal worship religion of these early Egyptian peoples included cats.
